turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Well, I guess what brings me in is that I feel like I’m just always moving from one thing to the next. Like I really can’t just idle, you know? And with the new work setup, it's gotten a lot harder to hide. 

They moved all of us customer service reps to this new open-plan office. I don't know whose idea that was, but it's terrible. Back in the day, we had actual tall cubicles. You could stand up, pace a little, fiddle with things without anyone noticing. Actually, my old cubicle had this desk with a wobbly leg, and I used to prop it up with a matchbook from this little diner down the street. Man, that diner had the absolute best cherry pie. It closed down, what, maybe five or six years ago? I think the owner retired and moved down to Florida. My brother lives in Florida, actually, near Tampa... 

But anyway, yeah... with the new office layout, everyone can see everything you do, and sitting perfectly still all day is just... well, it's not really working out for me.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient mentions a need to 'fiddle with things' and struggles with 'sitting perfectly still all day'.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes a habit of needing to 'stand up, pace a little' rather than remaining seated at work.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states feeling like they are 'always moving from one thing to the next' and 'can't just idle'.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting off-topic to discuss a wobbly desk, a diner, cherry pie, and their brother in Florida before returning to the main point.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the difficulty sitting still, do you find it hard to concentrate on tasks or keep your attention on one thing for a long period of time?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, concentration is... it's definitely a struggle. Like, if I have to sit through one of those long coaching meetings my supervisor likes to run, or if they hand us a new procedure to read, I start off totally fine. I'm right there with them. But then, after just a few minutes, I'll realize my eyes are still moving down the page, or the person is still talking, and I haven't actually taken in a single word they said. 

It's funny you mention reading, actually, because I used to read all the time when I was a kid. My mom would take me to the library every Saturday morning. We had this old station wagon, wood paneling on the sides, the whole nine yards. It smelled like peppermint because she always kept those little red and white candies in the glovebox. I tried to find those same candies the other day at the grocery store, but they just have these generic brand ones now, and they don't taste the same at all. They're kind of chalky, you know? 

But yeah, when it comes to work stuff, I just kind of zone out and have no idea what I just read or heard.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly states that concentration is a struggle and describes zoning out and losing focus after a few minutes during long meetings or when reading.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of reading work procedures to a detailed, unrelated story about childhood library trips, a station wagon, and peppermint candies.

turns.doctor_question: When you're at work or doing other tasks, do you find yourself acting or speaking without thinking first—like interrupting people, making quick decisions you later regret, or doing things on impulse? Or is the main struggle really just the restlessness and difficulty focusing?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, the impulse thing... that definitely happens, too. Like, I don't mean to be rude at all, but if I'm at my desk and I hear some of the other reps working through a complicated customer problem, I'll just jump right in. I'll blurt out the answer before they've even finished explaining the issue or, you know, before anyone even asked for my help. 

It's just that I usually know the answer right away because I've been there so long. I actually started at the company right after my buddy Rick got me the interview. Rick and I played softball together in this rec league for years. We were sponsored by this hardware store that used to be downtown... Miller's Hardware, I think it was called. Old man Miller was a real character. He used to sponsor our jerseys and everything, and he always insisted we wear these bright, neon orange shirts. We looked like a bunch of traffic cones running around the bases. I haven't seen Rick in a while, though. I think he got into woodworking or something in his garage. 

But anyway, yeah, I just kind of butt into their conversations at work without thinking. It just slips out.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they 'blurt out the answer before they've even finished explaining the issue'.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to jumping in and butting into coworkers' conversations without being asked.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient demonstrates tangential speech by drifting from a work topic to a long, unrelated story about a friend, a softball league, and a hardware store before returning to the point.

turns.doctor_question: How old were you when you first noticed these problems with sitting still, concentrating, and acting without thinking? Were these things going on when you were a kid in school, or did they really start showing up more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Well, looking back... it's definitely been around way longer than just this new office setup. I mean, even back when I was a kid in grade school, I remember my parents getting these report cards. The teachers would always write the exact same thing, year after year. They'd say I was a bright kid, but I was careless with my assignments, and I was always talking out of turn. They were constantly having to remind me to just sit down and stay with my work. 

Actually, speaking of grade school, my fourth-grade teacher was Mrs. Gable. She was this really strict lady who always wore these heavy wool cardigans, even when it was warm out. I remember she had this massive collection of porcelain frogs on her desk. Hundreds of them. Every time you walked past, they'd rattle against each other. My buddy Tommy accidentally knocked one over once and broke its leg off. He tried to glue it back on with that white paste we used for art projects, but it just looked like the frog had a cast on. Tommy was always getting into trouble, though. He ended up moving away in middle school, I think to Ohio or something. 

But yeah, the teachers were always telling my parents that I needed to pay better attention and stop blurting things out. So I guess it's been a thing for a really long time.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that teachers noted he was 'careless with my assignments' in grade school.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient mentions needing constant reminders to 'stay with my work' and 'pay better attention'.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient recalls that teachers constantly had to remind him to 'just sit down', indicating he was leaving his seat.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient states that teachers told his parents he needed to 'stop blurting things out'.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned these things were happening back in grade school. Do you remember if you were also physically restless and fidgety as a kid—like having trouble sitting still in class, or always needing to move around—or was it mainly just the talking out of turn and trouble paying attention?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, definitely. It wasn't just the talking out of turn. I was always squirming in my seat back then. And honestly, it never really stopped. Even today, when I’m sitting there trying to look completely calm and professional, my foot is just bouncing away under the desk. Or I’ll be in a meeting clicking a pen over and over, and I don't even notice I'm doing it until somebody gives me a look. 

Actually, speaking of pens, I used to have this absolute favorite one I’d click all the time. It was one of those heavy metal promotional ones I got from the local Chevy dealership when I bought my Silverado. Great truck, by the way. It had the extended cab, which was perfect because my wife and I used to take the dogs down to the lake on weekends. We had two Golden Retrievers, Buster and Daisy. Daisy loved the water, but Buster was terrified of it. He’d just stand on the dock barking at the ducks. The ducks down at that lake were completely fearless, though. People fed them so much bread they’d practically walk right up and eat out of your hand. I read somewhere recently that bread is actually really bad for ducks, though. Something about it lacking nutrients and messing up their wings? 

But anyway, yeah... I've always been a fidgeter. Bouncing my leg, clicking whatever is in my hand, all the way back to grade school.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about a promotional pen, his truck, dogs, and ducks before returning to the original topic.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly confirms a history and current presence of physical restlessness, including squirming in his seat, bouncing his foot, and clicking pens.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond what you've told me about school and work, have these problems with restlessness, concentration, and acting without thinking also caused you trouble in other areas of your life—like at home with family, in your relationships, or in other situations outside of work?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, it definitely spills over into home life, too. It's not just a work thing. Like, my wife and I will try to have a nice, quiet evening, you know? She loves to watch those historical dramas, the ones with the big dresses and the castles. And I try, I really do try to just sit there and watch it with her, or even just sit and read a book, but... I just can't do it for long. Before I know it, I'm shifting around on the couch, or I'm making comments about the show, or I just have to get up and grab a snack or check on something in the garage. 

Speaking of the garage, I finally got around to organizing my tool bench out there last weekend. It was a total disaster area. I had wrenches mixed in with the screwdrivers, and don't even get me started on the jars of random screws and nails I've collected over the years. I bought this heavy-duty pegboard from the hardware store—not Miller's, they closed down years ago, unfortunately. It's a big box store now, you know how it is. You can never find anyone to help you in those places. I spent twenty minutes just wandering the aisles looking for the right size masonry bits for my drill. I've got this old Black and Decker drill that still works like a charm. They don't make them like that anymore. 

But, uh, yeah... quiet stuff at home, like trying to relax with a movie or a book, it just doesn't last long before I'm up and moving around or talking through it.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes shifting around on the couch when trying to sit quietly.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions having to get up from his seat to grab a snack or check on things in the garage when expected to sit and watch a movie.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient explicitly states an inability to engage in quiet leisure activities, such as watching a movie or reading a book, without moving around or talking.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned these problems go back to grade school. Do you remember roughly how old you were when they first started, or were they pretty much there from the beginning of elementary school?
turns.patient_response:
Well, like I was saying before, it was definitely going on way before this whole new office thing started. I mean, it was pretty much right from the start of grade school, honestly. I remember my parents getting those report cards, probably starting around first or second grade, where the teachers would always write the exact same stuff. They'd say I was a bright kid, you know, but that I was careless with my assignments, and that I was always talking out of turn. They were constantly having to remind me to just stay with my work. 

Actually, speaking of first grade, we used to have this reading circle thing where we'd all sit on these little carpet squares. Mine was this bright mustard yellow color, which was my favorite because we had a kitchen floor that was almost that exact same shade. My mom had picked it out when we remodeled the house. She was really into that whole 70s aesthetic, lots of earth tones and macrame plant hangers everywhere. She had this huge spider plant hanging right over the kitchen sink that would always hit my dad in the head when he was doing the dishes. He complained about it constantly, but he never took it down because he knew she loved it. My dad was a good guy like that. Worked at the post office for thirty-something years before he retired. 

But yeah, the teachers were writing those things about me being careless and talking too much right from the beginning of elementary school. So it's been there basically the whole time.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that teachers noted they were 'careless with my assignments' starting in early elementary school.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient mentions that teachers constantly had to remind them to 'stay with my work,' indicating difficulty sustaining attention on tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states that teachers complained about them 'talking too much' and 'talking out of turn.'
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech during the response, drifting from a reading circle to carpet colors, kitchen remodels, house plants, and their father's career before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to those early report cards from first or second grade, do you remember roughly how old you were? And would you say the restlessness, trouble focusing, and blurting things out were all happening by the time you were around 12 years old?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, definitely before I was 12. Like I said, it was right there in those early report cards, so I would've been, what, six or seven years old? First or second grade. That's when they were already writing that I was bright but careless, and that I talked out of turn and needed reminding to stay on task. 

It's funny thinking about being seven. That was the year I got my first bicycle. It was a Schwinn Sting-Ray, the one with the banana seat and the high-rise handlebars. Man, I loved that bike. It was metallic blue. My older brother had a red one, but he crashed his into Mrs. Gable's rose bushes at the end of our street. Mrs. Gable was furious. She was this older lady who spent all day in her garden, wearing one of those big straw hats. She used to give out full-sized candy bars on Halloween, though, so we always tried to stay on her good side. Except for the rose bush incident, obviously. My brother had thorns in his arms for a week. 

But anyway, yeah, the trouble focusing, the blurting things out, the careless mistakes... it was all happening way back then, long before I was 12.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient confirms making 'careless mistakes' and being described as 'bright but careless' in early report cards.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient reports having 'trouble focusing' and needing 'reminding to stay on task' during childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly mentions 'blurting things out' and having 'talked out of turn' in early grades.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had periods where you felt unusually energetic, optimistic, or 'high' for several days in a row—where you needed less sleep than usual but still felt great, or where you were taking on a lot of projects or goals all at once with a lot of enthusiasm?
turns.patient_response:
No, I've never really had anything like that. I mean, I'll get into a project, sure, but not where I'm not sleeping or feeling unusually high or whatever. Like, I get excited about things sometimes. 

Actually, speaking of projects, I decided a few weeks ago I was going to finally fix the leaky faucet in the guest bathroom. It's been dripping for months, just this constant *drip, drip, drip*. Drives my wife crazy. So I watched a couple of YouTube videos—you can learn how to do anything on YouTube these days, it's amazing. I saw this one guy who built a whole log cabin just using hand tools. No power tools at all! He was out in the woods somewhere, maybe Canada? It looked freezing. He had this big bushy beard and wore flannel shirts every single day. I don't know how people live out in the middle of nowhere like that. I need to be close to a grocery store, you know? 

Anyway, I went to the hardware store to get the washers for the faucet, but then I remembered I needed a new air filter for the furnace, so I went to that aisle, and then I saw they had a sale on weather stripping... and I completely forgot the washers. So the faucet is still dripping. But yeah, no, I don't get those super energetic, no-sleep periods you're talking about. Just regular stuff.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility both in his tangential storytelling about YouTube videos and by getting sidetracked by other items at the hardware store.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes forgetting the primary purpose of his errand (buying washers) while at the hardware store.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies ever feeling 'unusually high' or having periods of elevated mood.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient denies having 'super energetic' periods.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly denies experiencing periods where he is 'not sleeping' or having 'no-sleep periods'.
symptom_reasoning.S040: The patient denies taking on projects with the unusual energy or lack of sleep described by the doctor.

turns.doctor_question: When you look back at your whole life—school, work, relationships, everything—would you say these problems with focusing, sitting still, and blurting things out have caused you real trouble or gotten in the way of things you wanted to do? Or have they been more of an annoyance that you've managed to work around?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's definitely gotten in the way, especially lately. Like, at work, it's actually started showing up in my performance reviews. My supervisors keep pointing out that I have all these unfinished tickets, and I'm making careless mistakes that end up slowing the whole team down. And it's frustrating because I'm really trying hard, you know? I generally get along great with the customers. I've always been a people person. 

Actually, I had this one customer last week, older guy, who called in because his internet was down. We ended up talking for like forty-five minutes about his grandson's little league team. They made it to the state championships! The kid plays shortstop, which was my position when I played in high school. I wasn't half bad, either. We had this coach, Coach Miller, who used to make us run foul poles until we puked if we missed a grounder. He was tough, but he really cared about us. He drove this beat-up old Ford truck that made a terrible grinding noise every time he shifted gears. I think the transmission was shot, but he refused to buy a new one. Said they didn't make 'em like they used to. 

But yeah, the work thing... it's a problem. Even though the customers like me, management is getting on my case about the unfinished tickets and the mistakes. So I guess you could say it's causing real trouble, not just an annoyance.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly states they are making careless mistakes at work.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions having unfinished tickets at work, indicating a failure to finish workplace duties.
